blocks.text: Yet, to say nothing of the New World, modern voyages teach us that they are also brought from Africa, though from its interior. Nor had this escaped Pliny, who in book 6, chapter 29, in the itinerary from Syene to the island of Meroë published by Nero's scouts, describing the island of Gagaudes, says: there parrots were first seen. This is confirmed by Paulus Venetus, writing about Abasia in book 3, chapter 45: It has parrots and very beautiful epimachi. But I cannot at all make sense of these words of Diodorus, book 2, page 95: Αἱ δὲ τῆς Συρίας ἐσχατιαὶ ψιττακοὺς, καὶ πορφυρίωνας, καὶ μελεαγρίδας (ἐκτρέφουσι) [Hai de tēs Syrias eschatiai psittakous, kai porphyriōnas, kai meleagridas (ektrephousi)]. For it is a paradoxical claim, and indeed plainly false, that parrots are born in Syria. I therefore suspect that the passage is corrupt, although what should be restored does not occur to me.
